title: Mechanical Activation of Terahertz Tunneling in Metallic Nanogaps
authors: Dasom Kim, Dukhyung Lee, Young-Mi Bahk, Dai-Sik Kim
abstract: Metallic nanogaps concentrate terahertz (THz) fields into deep subwavelength volumes and support field-driven electron tunneling when the insulating barrier becomes sufficiently narrow. Here, we demonstrate mechanical control of tunneling-mediated nonlinear THz transmission in a flexible nanogap metasurface. The metasurface consists of Au/PMMA/Au nanogaps fabricated on a polyethylene terephthalate substrate, enabling continuous tuning of the gap geometry through macroscopic bending. In the flat state, the resonant transmission exhibits only a weak dependence on the incident THz field strength. Upon bending, increasing the incident field strength induces pronounced resonance suppression accompanied by saturation of the voltage developed across the nanogaps. This nonlinear response is consistent with the opening of a field-dependent tunneling conduction channel through the mechanically narrowed PMMA barriers. Simmons-model calculations illustrate the strong increase in tunneling current density and the associated dissipative gap response as the local gap width approaches the few-nanometer regime. These results establish mechanical deformation as a macroscopic means of controlling tunneling-mediated THz nonlinearities in flexible metasurfaces.
summary: This work reports on controlling nonlinear THz transmission in flexible metallic nanogaps by physically bending the structure. Bending mechanically narrows the insulating barrier, activating a tunneling conduction channel. This transition shifts the junction's electrical behavior from a linear capacitive response to a nonlinear, tunneling-dominated regime, demonstrating mechanical control over quantum electronic properties.
main_problem: The paper demonstrates the ability to control nonlinear Terahertz (THz) tunneling-mediated transmission in metallic nanogaps by applying macroscopic mechanical strain.
main_result: Mechanical bending transitions the junction from a capacitive regime (flat state) to a tunneling-dominated regime (bent state), causing pronounced resonance suppression and voltage saturation.
method: The study combines THz time-domain spectroscopy measurements with theoretical modeling using the Simmons tunneling model and structural mechanics simulations.
model_or_system: The system is an Au/PMMA/Au nanogap metasurface fabricated on a flexible PET substrate. The physics involves modeling the junction as a parallel combination of capacitance and field-dependent tunneling conductance.
key_observables: THz transmittance spectra, gap voltage ($V_{gap}$), tunneling current density ($J_{tun}$), and the imaginary part of the effective dielectric constant ($	ext{Im}\{\epsilon_{gap}\}$).
important_parameters: Gap width (approaching the few-nanometer regime), incident THz field strength (up to 150 kV/cm), and bending curvature/radius.
main_assumptions: The gap voltage estimation uses an area-averaging approximation based on the Kirchhoff integral formalism, and the local barrier width is approximated as 1 nm for tunneling calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the fabrication process, the effect of bending on geometry (structural simulations), and the THz transmittance spectra showing systematic nonlinear suppression in the bent state compared to the flat state.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system, details the mechanical and electrical characterization methods, presents the comparison between the flat (capacitive) and bent (tunneling) states, and concludes by linking macroscopic mechanical control to ultrafast nanoscale nonlinear THz response.
why_interesting: The coupling of macroscopic mechanical deformation to ultrafast, nonlinear quantum tunneling phenomena at THz frequencies provides a novel, tunable platform for studying charge transport in nanoscale junctions.
